newsitem.title: USA: Gateway 2000 unveils low-cost corporate PC.
newsitem.headline: Gateway 2000 unveils low-cost corporate PC.

text.p: Gateway 2000 Inc. a direct marketer of personal computers, on Wednesday unveiled a network PC that costs under $1,000 as part of a product line aimed at capturing a greater share of the corporate PC market.
The new network PC, called the E-1000, is designed to provide customers with a PC that lowers their total costs of ownership.

Gateway unveiled its new products one day ahead of its move to the New York Stock Exchange, where its shares will begin trading Thursday under the symbol GTW. Gateway now trades on the Nasdaq, where its stock has been volatile in recent months.

Gateway founder, Chairman and CEO Ted Waitt will ring the opening bell at the NYSE. The North Sioux City, S.D.-based company plans to bring a cow, the company's motif on its PC boxes, business cards and stationery, to the trading floor.
Gateway executives said they toyed with the idea of having MOO as the company's stock symbol, but decided not to.
A NYSE spokesman said this will be the first time a cow has visited the New York Stock Exchange trading floor.
"We hope that everything works out," the spokesman said.
The move to the NYSE is also an attempt to portray the company as a stable firm in a push to invade some of the turf occupied by rival Dell Computer Corp..
"Like it or not some investors still go to the Big Board first," said Louis Mazzucchelli of Gerard Klauer & Mattison.

Gateway's large accounts make up about 36 percent of total sales, with all business, including small business customers, making up some 49 percent of total sales. Waitt emphasized that Gateway already has corporate customers, but it hopes to become a larger presence in that more profitable sector.

But some analysts said Gateway faces some obstacles with big corporate users, because it does not yet have a server computer offering and because of the company's "silicon cowboy" image. Gateway said, however, that it is considering entering the market for servers, which run computer networks.

"What they need to do a better job of is branding," said Richard Schutte, a Goldman Sachs analyst. "The cows are not going to work in the corporate market. They must create a brand identity away from the cow, toward more of the mainstream."
But Waitt said Gateway has no plans to give up the cows.
"No way," he told reporters when asked about some suggestions that Gateway "lose the cows" to target business. "We are not going to change who we are, we are proud of it."
Gateway also said it will double its sales force to about 800 people by the year's end to address the corporate market.
"(The sales staff) is on its way to roughly 800 to support corporate customers," Waitt said.
The E Series, including the E 1000, are aimed at the corporate "enterprise" and all are designed around Intel Corp. Pentium processors.
Gateway said an E-1000 PC with a monitor starts at $1,249, although prices may vary depending on quantity. Large quantity orders for PCs without monitors are below $900.

The standard system includes a 166MHz Pentium processor, 16 megabytes of memory, a 1.2 gigabyte hard disk drive and a the capability to be networked to other PCs. Gateway expects to ship the E-1000 in July.
